rationale: These recordings have had no artifact rejection, so the mean-averaged Welch PSD is pulled around by a few windows with blinks, movement or muscle bursts. That is likely worse on the external clinics' short 1-minute recordings. Taking the median across the 2-s Welch windows (`average="median"`) gives a robust estimate of each subject's typical resting spectrum, which should give cleaner relative band powers (e.g. schizophrenia's extra delta/theta and reduced alpha) without changing the feature set or the classifier.

I'm adding one per-channel aperiodic (1/f) exponent to the existing relative band powers. It is the slope of log-power against log-frequency over 2–40 Hz, fitted with the 7–14 Hz alpha peak left out. Schizophrenia has been linked to a flatter spectrum (a shift in cortical excitation/inhibition balance), which band powers only capture indirectly. Because the exponent is a slope in log space, it doesn't depend on amplitude scale or recording length, which should help on the external amplifiers.

I'm adding one feature per channel: the individual alpha frequency (IAF). It is the centre of gravity of the 7–13 Hz power that sits above the subject's own fitted 1/f background, computed from the slope fit we already have. Slower alpha is one of the most consistently replicated resting-EEG findings in schizophrenia. The relative-power and slope features miss it because they lump all of 8–13 Hz into one band. A frequency also doesn't depend on amplitude scale, reference or recording length, so it should carry over to the external sets. This hasn't been run yet, so I have no score for it.

Schizophrenia is often described as a dysconnectivity disorder, and the current features only describe each channel on its own. I'm adding one connectivity measure: each channel's mean debiased-style weighted phase-lag index (wPLI) to all other channels, in the theta, alpha and beta bands, computed from 2-s Hann-windowed epochs. wPLI uses only the imaginary part of the cross-spectrum, so zero-lag volume conduction and a shared reference don't inflate it. It is a ratio, so it doesn't depend on amplitude scale, and it is averaged over epochs, so recording length matters little. Averaging per channel adds 48 features per condition rather than 360 pairwise values, which keeps the model small for n≈100.

I'm adding EEG microstate features. Abnormal microstate dynamics in schizophrenia (more class C, less class D) are among the most replicated resting-state findings, and none of the current spectral or connectivity features capture them. Four group template maps are learned label-free with polarity-invariant modified k-means on GFP peaks pooled across all subjects (2–20 Hz, average-referenced). Each subject's recording is then back-fitted to the templates to get coverage, mean duration and occurrence rate per class. These measures don't depend on amplitude scale, reference or recording length.

I'm adding one feature per channel: the Higuchi fractal dimension of the 1–45 Hz band-passed signal. It is computed on 4-s epochs, and the median across epochs is kept. Altered EEG complexity is a well-replicated finding in schizophrenia, and the current spectral and wPLI features don't measure signal complexity directly. Fractal dimension doesn't depend on amplitude scale. Filtering removes drift and line noise, and taking the median over epochs damps artifacts and makes recording length matter little. Both should help on the external sets. This hasn't been run yet, so I have no score for it.

I'm adding a covariance-matrix description of the signal in Riemannian tangent space. Each recording is band-passed to 1–45 Hz and split into 4-s epochs. High-power artifact epochs are dropped, and the rest are averaged into a 16×16 covariance. That covariance is trace-normalized and lightly shrunk, then mapped to the tangent space at the training fold's log-Euclidean mean, and the result is added to the existing features. Schizophrenia's dysconnectivity includes zero-lag coupling and changes in how power is spread across the scalp. Per-channel wPLI strength discards both by design, and covariance in tangent space captures them in a way that is well established for small-n EEG classification. Trace normalization keeps the features independent of amplitude scale, and averaging over epochs makes recording length matter little.

With eyes closed, the broadband 1–45 Hz covariance is dominated by alpha and slow power, so the tangent-space features mostly describe alpha topography. This change adds two more trace-normalized covariances, from theta (4–8 Hz) and beta (13–30 Hz) band-passed epochs, each with the same artifact-epoch rejection and mapped to the Riemannian tangent space. The hypothesis is that schizophrenia's dysconnectivity is frequency-specific (excess frontal theta coupling, altered beta) and is currently washed out. This hasn't been run yet, so I have no score for it.

I'm adding a delta-band (1–4 Hz) covariance to the filter bank, trace-normalized, with the same artifact-epoch rejection, and mapped to the Riemannian tangent space like the others. Excess slow-wave (delta) activity, mostly frontal, is one of the most replicated resting-EEG findings in schizophrenia. In the broadband covariance, delta topography is mixed with the dominant eyes-closed alpha, and relative band power records only each channel's delta level, not its spatial coupling. A separate delta covariance should capture that pattern while staying independent of amplitude scale.

There are about 80 training subjects and about 584 standardized features. Under one shared L2 penalty, the 408 tangent-space covariance features carry most of the model's total feature variance. So the small, well-established per-channel marker families (aperiodic slope, IAF and HFD, 16 features each) are effectively shrunk away. This change rescales each feature family block after standardization so every block contributes equal total variance, which works like a group-balanced prior; total variance and C stay the same. I haven't run it, so it has no score yet.

I'm adding one feature per channel: normalized permutation entropy (order 4, lag 2 samples, so it emphasizes activity below about 32 Hz). It is computed on the existing artifact-damped 1–45 Hz 4-s epochs, and the median across epochs is kept. Altered ordinal-pattern complexity is a replicated resting-EEG marker in schizophrenia. It captures the temporal irregularity of the signal's shape, which Higuchi FD (curve-length scaling) and the spectral features don't, and since it depends only on rank order, it is immune to amplitude scale and to the amplifier. The block-balanced prior gives it its own equal-variance slot. This hasn't been run yet, so I have no score for it.

C=0.1 was fixed before the feature set grew. The model now has 3 tangent-space covariances, wPLI, HFD and block-balanced variance weights, so the right penalty strength has probably moved. This change picks C for each training fold from a log grid (0.01–1). The choice is made by repeated stratified-grouped inner CV AUROC on that fold's subjects (`ctx["groups_train"]`), with ties going to the stronger penalty. The aim is shrinkage matched to n≈80 instead of a hand-set value. I haven't run it, so it has no score yet.

I'm splitting the relative-power bands into low/high alpha (8–10 / 10–13 Hz) and low/high beta (13–20 / 20–30 Hz), so there are 7 bands instead of 5. Schizophrenia's resting-EEG findings are sub-band specific: power shifts from upper to lower alpha, and fast beta2 activity increases (partly linked to medication). The single wide alpha and beta bands average these opposite effects away. The ratios still don't depend on amplitude scale, and because the relative-power block keeps its equal-variance weight, the rest of the model's balance stays the same. I haven't run this, so it has no Dev score yet.

I'm adding one feature per channel: the long-range temporal correlation (DFA exponent) of the alpha-band (8–13 Hz) amplitude envelope, fitted over windows of 1–10 s. Reduced LRTC of alpha oscillations is a replicated schizophrenia finding (Nikulin et al. 2012). It describes how stable the alpha rhythm is over time, which none of the current time-averaged spectral, wPLI, HFD or covariance features capture. A scaling exponent also doesn't depend on amplitude scale, and it gets its own equal-variance block. This hasn't been run yet, so I have no Dev score for it.

I'm adding a second connectivity measure: each channel's orthogonalized amplitude-envelope correlation (Hipp et al. 2012 AEC) node strength in the theta, alpha and beta bands, as its own block with equal variance weight. Schizophrenia's dysconnectivity shows up in slow co-fluctuations of band-limited amplitude as well as in phase coupling. wPLI measures only phase, and the covariance block measures only zero-lag coupling. Orthogonalizing each signal pair removes zero-lag leakage and the effect of the shared reference, and because the measure is a correlation it doesn't depend on amplitude scale.

With eyes closed, the broadband 1–45 Hz covariance mixes alpha with high-amplitude frontal delta and eye-movement power, so the model never sees a clean alpha-band spatial coupling. That is notable because reduced and spatially altered alpha is a core resting-EEG finding in schizophrenia. This change adds an alpha-band (8–13 Hz) covariance, using the same artifact-epoch rejection, trace normalization and Riemannian tangent mapping as the others, which completes the theta/alpha/beta filter bank. The delta covariance (round 9) was tried before block balancing existed; this new block gets its own equal-variance slot, so it doesn't swamp the small per-channel marker families. I haven't run this, so it has no Dev score yet.

I'm adding a periodic-power block (16 channels × 3 bands = 48 features, each block with its own equal-variance weight). For each channel it measures how far the theta (4–7 Hz), alpha (7–14 Hz) and beta (14–30 Hz) peaks rise above that channel's own fitted 1/f background. The current relative band powers mix the oscillation with the 1/f background, so a flatter 1/f slope and a weaker alpha rhythm can look alike. Separating the two (as in Donoghue et al. 2020) should isolate the reduced alpha and altered beta rhythms reported in schizophrenia. The peak height is a difference of log powers, so it doesn't depend on amplitude scale or recording length. This hasn't been run, so I have no Dev score for it yet.

I'm adding Hjorth mobility and complexity per channel as two new blocks, each with its own equal-variance weight. Both are log-transformed medians over the existing artifact-damped 1–45 Hz 4-s epochs. Mobility tracks each channel's mean frequency, and complexity tracks how widely the spectrum is spread. The slowed, broadened resting spectrum reported in schizophrenia should show up in these. Neither is captured by band-limited power ratios or by Higuchi FD, which measures curve-length scaling. Both are variance ratios, so they don't depend on amplitude scale, and the median over epochs makes them robust to artifacts and recording length. I haven't run this, so it has no Dev score yet.

I'm replacing the per-channel wPLI node strength (16 values per band) with the full pairwise wPLI upper triangle (120 values per band) for theta, alpha and beta. The pairwise values keep one equal-variance slot together, so the family's weight in the model doesn't change. Schizophrenia's lagged dysconnectivity is reported as pair-specific (e.g. fronto-temporal versus posterior pairs). Averaging each channel over all its partners can cancel opposite changes and blur that topography. The covariance tangent-space blocks only see zero-lag coupling, so they don't recover it. Pairwise wPLI is still independent of amplitude scale and volume conduction.

I'm adding a low-gamma (30–45 Hz) spatial covariance to the filter bank, completing it above beta. It uses the same artifact-epoch rejection, trace normalization and Riemannian tangent mapping as the other bands, and gets its own equal-variance block slot. Raised resting fast/gamma activity and altered gamma coupling are reported in schizophrenia, and the per-channel relative gamma power we already have doesn't capture how that activity is coupled across the scalp. Each band-specific covariance added so far has improved Dev, and trace normalization keeps this block independent of amplitude scale. I haven't run this, so it has no Dev score yet.
